title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
I was recently recommended "YourBench: Easy Custom Evaluation Sets for Everyone" by Sumuk Shashidhar and others. It was a great read and tackles something we all deal with. Here's what it's about.
Static benchmarks are becoming the flip phones of AI evaluation📱
We're stuck with evaluation methods that can't keep pace with how quickly this field moves. Static benchmarks saturate within months, get contaminated by training data, and become irrelevant as knowledge evolves. Meanwhile, manual evaluation is expensive and slow, creating a bottleneck just when we need rapid, domain-specific assessment most.
YourBench tackles this by automatically generating fresh, document-grounded evaluation sets from any collection of documents you provide. The approach works by preprocessing documents into semantic chunks, using LLM ensembles to generate diverse question-answer pairs with verifiable citations, then filtering for quality and removing duplicates. Within minutes and for under $2 per domain, you get challenging, contamination-resistant benchmarks tailored to your specific needs.
The authors uncovered an interesting validity-diversity tradeoff: models like o3 mini excel at generating clear, answerable questions (96% validity) but with low semantic diversity, while others like Qwen2.5 32B achieve high diversity (93%) but sacrifice some validity. DeepSeek V3 strikes a nice balance, scoring well on both dimensions (90% diversity, 90% validity).
The validation results are compelling: when they replicated 7 MMLU subsets using just Wikipedia pages, the synthetic benchmarks perfectly preserved model rankings (Spearman ρ=1.0) while being consistently harder than the originals. That said, there are limitations—they only tested a subset of MMLU domains without clear selection criteria, validation was limited to MMLU rather than multiple benchmarks, and open models were capped at 70B. I'd be curious to see how this approach performs with frontier models and broader benchmark validation.
🔗 Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gz1Pw0sXcAAiLyw.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Just read OpenAI's paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate" and there's crucial insights buried in the technical details that affects everyone using these systems.
Quick summary: Large language models often make up plausible-sounding but incorrect information when they're unsure about something, rather than admitting they don't know. This happens because during training, models learn that guessing confidently usually gets rewarded more than saying "I'm not certain," and current evaluation methods don't penalize models for being confidently wrong.
OpenAI
During pretraining, even with perfect training data, models will generate errors due to the cross-entropy objective they're optimizing. The authors show that generating valid text is fundamentally harder than simply classifying whether existing text is valid or invalid. Think of it this way: if you can't reliably tell the difference between correct and incorrect statements in a classification task, how can you expect to generate only correct statements? This creates a mathematical lower bound on errors.
The persistence after post-training comes down to incentive alignment: Binary evaluation metrics reward confident guessing over honest uncertainty. A model that always says "I'm 95% sure the answer is X" will consistently outperform one that appropriately says "I don't know" when uncertain.
But here's what really caught my attention: our evaluation methods are fundamentally broken. Most benchmarks use binary scoring (correct = 1, wrong = 0) that penalizes uncertainty expressions like "I don't know." This creates perverse incentives where confident guessing beats honest uncertainty every time.
The authors suggest changing how we score AI performance. For multiple choice evaluations, instead of the standard 1 for correct and 0 for wrong, they propose: 1 for correct, 0 for "I don't know," and -1 for wrong answers. I'd argue we might want a small penalty like -0.1 for uncertainty to still incentivize attempts.
An alternative approach: models could provide confidence scores alongside answers, essentially "betting" on their responses. Higher confidence means more points to gain or lose—similar to how a confident gambler risks more.
What strikes me is that in the field we haven't really thought deeply about scoring mechanisms for MC evaluations. Negative scores for wrong answers are standard in university exams, yet major AI benchmarks haven't adopted this approach.
What would model rankings look like if we implemented these changes?

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Last week I ran some inference speed benchmarking with vLLM. Here are three tidbits I found interesting:
1. The model you select can make or break your speed!
Qwen3 4B gets a throughput of 2570 output tokens/s whereas Gemma3 4B achieves 4670. That's an almost 2x speedup!
2. Boost your model's speed with tensor parallelism!
So far I thought that TP is only necessary if your model doesn't fit on one GPU. But since TP reduces the size of matrix multiplications on each GPU, it can speed up inference if the matrices are very large (which is the case in larger models). I tested all Gemma3 models and found that for models up to 4B, using tensor parallelism (TP) negatively impacts performance. For the 12B model, TP2 is optimal, while for the 27B model, TP4 is best.
In the case of the 12B model, the speedup is approximately 1/8, increasing from 1,160 to 1,330 output tokens/s. The speedup for the 27B model is remarkable: from 310 (TP1) to 670 (TP2) to 700 (TP4) output tokens/s. With 16K input and 4K output tokens, the speedup is nearly 4x from TP1 to TP4.
3. max_num_seqs did not really vary between 128 and 256. For max_num_batched_tokens I didn't really see a pattern of what worked well but the variations were usually minor.
I ran these experiments with 4K input tokens and 3K output tokens using vllm's autotune script on NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80GB GPUs. Measurements are normalized to one GPU. Results vary depending on factors such as input and output length, vllm version and settings or hardware.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G1DldVQaoAAVJaM.jpg

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Clementine just dropped an incredibly useful guide to evaluations in 2025 ✨
The key insight: we're transitioning from testing knowledge retention to measuring practical problem-solving ability. Her framework spans core capabilities, integrated assistant tasks, adaptive scenarios, and even forecasting - all focused on whether models can actually accomplish useful work rather than just demonstrate what they've learned.
One domain that deserves more attention in this evolution is legal AI. Law represents a perfect storm for LLM evaluation: high-stakes accuracy requirements, complex multi-step reasoning, and almost entirely text-based workflows. Yet major model providers consistently overlook legal capabilities in their evaluations. A few key evals worth tracking:
LegalBench (2023) contains 162 lawyer-authored tasks testing issue spotting, rule recall, rule application, rule conclusion, interpretation, and rhetorical reasoning. Tasks include multiple-choice, classification, and open-ended QA, with evaluation by accuracy or expert judgment. It is widely used for pretraining-style evaluation but many tasks are now relatively easy for strong LLMs.
LEXam (2025) evaluates law school exam questions through thousands of multiple-choice and open-ended problems. MCQs are scored by accuracy, while open answers are judged with an LLM-as-judge against reference reasoning chains. The MCQs are suited for pretraining evaluation, while the open-ended section remains a hard post-training benchmark.
LexSumm (2024) aggregates eight summarization datasets including BillSum, EurLexSum, GovReport, MultiLexSum (tiny, short, long), InAbs, and UKAbs. Models generate summaries compared with human references across jurisdictions and granularities. Evaluation uses ROUGE, BERTScore, and measures like compression ratio, coverage, and density, making it a strong post-training test.
Recent retrieval datasets test whether models can locate precise legal passages and ground reasoning in them. LePaRD (2023) emphasizes passage-level retrieval from case law with Recall@K metrics, CLERC (2024) combines citation recovery with retrieval-augmented generation scored by Recall@K, nDCG, ROUGE, and citation precision/recall, and Bar Exam QA with Housing Statute QA (2025) require retrieving gold passages to answer questions, evaluated by recall and QA accuracy.
What's missing is more dynamic, realistic legal evaluation - something equivalent to the assistant tasks Clementine describes but grounded in actual legal workflows. Think: drafting contracts with changing requirements, conducting legal research across multiple jurisdictions, or managing document review with adversarial conditions. Time for evaluation methods that reflect these real-world demands. ⚖️
Quoting @clefourrier
Updated the evaluation guidebook with a new deep dive!
2025 panorama of all the important and next level evaluations that you need to know to build *actually impactful and useful* models!
(Assistant tasks, games, forecasting, and more)

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Getting 10x speedup in #vLLM is easier than you think 📈
I just discovered speculative decoding with ngram lookup and the results speak for themselves. Here's what you add to your vLLM serve command:
speculative_config={
"method": "ngram",
"num_speculative_tokens": 8,
"prompt_lookup_max": 7,
}
The intuition is straightforward: there's often high n-gram overlap between your prompt and the LLM's output. Entity names, phrases, or code chunks get copied directly from input to output. Prompt lookup exploits this pattern by searching your prompt for n-gram sequences that match what the model is likely to generate next.
When it finds matches, it proposes multiple tokens at once and verifies them with the main model - processing accepted tokens together for the speedup.
This works particularly well for:
- Document summarization and QA
- Code editing and refactoring
- Any input-grounded generation task
Key implementation details:
- prompt_lookup_max (7): Maximum n-gram length to search for
- num_speculative_tokens (8): Candidate tokens to propose
- highest speedup achieved with +1 relationship between these parameters
- No model modifications required, maintains output quality
I've been testing this on document rephrasing with gemma-3-12b-it across two H100s, processing fineweb documents where input-output overlap is substantial. Tuning beyond the defaults (5,4) to (8,7) gave me an additional 90 tokens/sec, with a draft acceptance rate of 70%.
The performance gains make the simple configuration change well worth it.
Anyone else experimenting with this? Would love to hear the results on your tasks! 🔬

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Following up on @OpenAI's recent paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate," I wondered how their proposed scoring changes would affect actual benchmark performance. So I ran the experiment myself 🧪
I modified GPQA Diamond to include "I don't know" as option E and implemented the paper's suggested scoring: +1 for correct answers, 0 for admitting uncertainty, and -1 for confident wrong answers. The instructions explicitly told models that mistakes are penalized while "I don't know" gets neutral points.
The results mostly mirror traditional accuracy rankings, but with one interesting reversal: GPT-5 edges out Gemini 2.5 Pro on the new scoring despite Pro leading on traditional accuracy. Pro never abstains (idk frequency ≈ 0), while GPT-5 shows more appropriate uncertainty. Smaller models like GPT-5 nano abstain more frequently, which actually helps their scores compared to confidently wrong larger models. The gap between traditional and uncertainty-aware scoring varies meaningfully across models—suggesting some are better calibrated than others.
Thanks for the discussions Lewis Tunstall, Clémentine Fourrier, Nathan Habib, Hynek Kydlíček!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G18RsBfbAAE_E-P.png

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)

Finally seeing some movement on the kind of evals that actually matter 🎯
GDPval is a benchmark that measures how well AI models perform on economically valuable, real-world tasks across major knowledge work occupations by comparing their outputs to expert human deliverables. It uses blind grading to benchmark AI against professionals on tasks like legal briefs and engineering designs. This helps track practical progress and shows how models can generate real economic value in workplaces.

summary:
I am looking forward to presenting our work "LEXam: Benchmarking Legal Reasoning on 340 Law Exams at the Data Science Talk Series @ UNT!
Thanks Haihua Chen for the invitation!
Abstract:
Long-form legal reasoning remains a key challenge for large language models (LLMs) in spite of recent advances in test-time scaling. To address this, we introduce \textsc{LEXam}, a novel benchmark derived from 340 law exams spanning 116 law school courses across a range of subjects and degree levels. The dataset comprises 4,886 law exam questions in English and German, including 2,841 long-form, open-ended questions and 2,045 multiple-choice questions. Besides reference answers, the open questions are also accompanied by explicit guidance outlining the expected legal reasoning approach such as issue spotting, rule recall, or rule application. Our evaluation on both open-ended and multiple-choice questions present significant challenges for current LLMs; in particular, they notably struggle with open questions that require structured, multi-step legal reasoning. Moreover, our results underscore the effectiveness of the dataset in differentiating between models with varying capabilities. Deploying an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm with rigorous human expert validation, we demonstrate how model-generated reasoning steps can be evaluated consistently and accurately, closely aligning with human expert assessments. Our evaluation setup provides a scalable method to assess legal reasoning quality beyond simple accuracy metrics. We have open-sourced our code on GitHub and released our data on the Hugging Face hub.
We welcome contributions to extend LEXam, please let us know if you're interested!

summary:
Very cool and detailed @Stanford and @CarnegieMellon study on sycophancy: "Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence"
Sycophancy, the phenomenon of excessively agreeing with or flattering users, is a pervasive issue in current LLMs.
Findings:
- AI models are significantly more sycophantic than humans, affirming users’ actions 50% more often, even in scenarios involving manipulation or harm.
- Interaction with sycophantic AI models decreases willingness to repair interpersonal conflicts and increases users' conviction that they are in the right, even when consensus judgments indicate the user is wrong.
- Participants prefer sycophantic AI responses, rating them as higher quality, more trustworthy, and expressing greater willingness to use those models again.
- These user preferences risk creating incentives for further sycophancy in AI training, potentially entrenching biases and discouraging prosocial behavior, highlighting the need for explicit mitigation strategies.
This is a great example of very thorough and methodologically high-quality work: cool to see them preregistering their experiments, something very rare in ML research. Preregistration is the practice of publicly documenting your research plan, including hypotheses, methods, and analysis strategies, before conducting the study to reduce publication bias and improve transparency. According to a small analysis I ran on this year's ArXiv papers, less than 0.1% of papers in mention preregistration in the abstract!

[1/2] Stop what you are doing and try out GEPA now!
"GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning" presents such elegant ideas by a collection of amazing researchers!
Here is a tldr of how it works:
GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) is a sample-efficient prompt optimization method for compound AI systems that works by reflectively evolving prompts using natural language feedback instead of traditional scalar rewards. In each iteration, GEPA samples system rollouts (including reasoning traces, tool outputs, and any diagnostic text), reflects on them via an LLM to identify issues or propose improvements, and updates specific module prompts accordingly based on the feedback. To ensure diversity and avoid local optima, GEPA maintains a pool of candidates and uses Pareto-based selection, which keeps all non-dominated strategies discovered so far and stochastically proposes new prompt variants, enabling robust generalization with far fewer rollouts than reinforcement learning methods.
I love the combination of Pareto-based selection, LLM reflection, and genetic algorithms. And it outperforms GRPO on four benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, Hover, PUPA) by simply optimizing the prompt!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Reasoning models excel at math but struggle with simple requests like word limits during thinking
TLDR: Models ignore user instructions while reasoning despite following them in final outputs.
Users need control over format, language, and length for transparency, auditability, and cost management. Current reasoning models excel at correct answers but fail to respect constraints during their thinking process.
@togethercompute researchers tested six reasoning models (GPT-OSS, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, GLM-4.5) on 300 math and science problems with verifiable instructions like word limits, multilingual reasoning, and JSON formatting. The best model scored 25% in instruction following during reasoning versus 79% in final responses. Harder problems worsened compliance. Simple multi-turn feedback ("you didn't follow the instruction, try again") boosted scores 17% on average. Finetuning improved GPT-OSS-20B instruction following from 11% to 27%.
Some thoughts:
- The multi-turn result is wild. Just telling the model it failed doubles compliance in some cases without any training
- The task difficulty correlation is concerning. When you most need structured reasoning (hard problems), models are least likely to follow rules
- 27% after finetuning is still bad. We might need architecture-level changes or fundamentally different training
- Related work on MathIF found the same tension, suggesting this is systemic to how we train reasoning models

Cool analogy regarding training on the test task
"The 1968 Olympics took place in Mexico City at the significant altitude of 2340 meters, higher than Australia’s tallest peak. Runners who had trained at altitude in their home countries were better prepared to compete in Mexico City’s conditions, as it turned out. But the hotly debated results of the Games did not lead the organizers to prohibit training at natural altitude. Instead, they let everyone do it, and athletes came to consider altitude training an excellent way to train.
The anecdote holds a lesson for the evaluation of large language models half a century later. Knowledge about the evaluation conditions necessarily influences training practices under competitive pressure. It may be a fool’s errand to prohibit the practice. Instead, we propose to adjust for it by giving every model the same task-specific preparation before evaluation. We work from the assumption that training on the test task, in general, cannot be effectively detected, disallowed, or disincentivized. Detecting what training data a model has seen is a notoriously difficult problem –existing heuristics achieve partial success at best. Researchers routinely acknowledge the futility of fighting data contamination. Moreover, we anticipate that the ways to effectively train on the test task will only grow in scope and adoption."

Gemini-3 achieved the top spot on most major benchmarks last week, but how well does it know the law? Unfortunately, most model providers don't evaluate on law-specific benchmarks. So while we have a good idea of how good new models are at coding, we are pretty much in the dark about their lawyering abilities.
This is why we ran a vibe-check on six diverse datasets from Greek bar exams over Indian law questions to Swiss university law exams among others. So what do the vibes say?
AA-Omniscience: 6/10 – high competence but unreliable
LegalBench: 9.5/10 – almost perfect answers
GreekBarBench: 9/10 – impressive long-context reasoning without hallucinations
IndianLawQA: 8.5/10 – The task feels precise, clean, and insightful, revealing how reliably Gemini-3 handles high-precision statutory queries (including new BNSS 2023 codes) while most models typically hallucinate in this domain.
WilfulMisconduct: 8/10 – strong logic, missed binding precedent
LEXam: 7/10 – competent but overly confident
Gemini-3 is extremely strong at many legal tasks and often performs at or above the level of very good human lawyers. However, it still makes serious mistakes: it often answers confidently even when it does not know the right legal rule or fact, instead of saying “I don’t know.” Because of this overconfidence and some failures on complex reasoning and precedents, it cannot safely replace human lawyers and still needs expert oversight.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
10% improvement on GPQA with one simple trick: asking multiple models the same question. Time to revisit ensembles?
I tested simple majority vote ensembles on GPQA Diamond using the "idk setup" (where incorrect answers get -1 points, correct answers are rewarded, and abstentions receive 0 points).
Ensembling the top-3 models I tested (Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and GPT-5 Mini) significantly outperforms each individual model. The ensemble achieves 86 on the traditional score and 75 on the idk score, nearly 7 points (almost 10%) better than the previous best individual model.
We're slowly rediscovering what ensemble methods can do for LLMs. Here are two compelling examples:
1. @karpathy's LLM Council: A local web app that sends your question to multiple LLMs via OpenRouter, displays their individual answers, has them critique and rank each other, then lets a designated "chairman" model synthesize a final response.
2. Cursor 2.0 Multi-Agent Mode: Multiple coding agents run in parallel on separate git worktrees or machines, with tools to quickly review, test, and iteratively fix their code, letting you pick the best result for harder tasks.
Curious to hear about your LLM ensemble applications!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
🚨 Plot twist: When AI gets it "wrong," your data might be the problem
When evaluating LEXam-idk, we noticed something strange: on several questions, the top 5 models (Gemini-3 Pro, Qwen3 Max, Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V3.1 Terminus) all gave the same wrong answer.
That seemed statistically unlikely, so we dug deeper.
Turns out, they weren't wrong. Our data was.
@yu_fan_768, Jakob Merane and Luka Nenadic did the heavy lifting on this debugging work. They found wrong human labels from the original data and unclear question stems. After cleaning the data and improving question clarity (e.g., "whether the following statements are correct" → "which of the following statements are correct"), the mystery solved itself.
The takeaway? Modern LLMs are now so capable that when multiple top models agree on a "wrong" answer, it's a signal worth investigating. The bug might not be in the models. It could be in your ground truth data, unclear instructions, or evaluation setup.
Model consensus is becoming a debugging tool for benchmark quality.
TL;DR: When 5 top AI models agree on the wrong answer, check your data first. They might be right, and your labels might be wrong. Modern LLMs are now good enough that their consensus can expose bugs in your benchmarks.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
GPT-5.2 sets new SOTA on LEXam-IDK! 📊
Fresh benchmarks show GPT-5.2 achieving 88.85% on traditional scoring and 78.19% on LEXam-IDK; narrowly edging out Gemini 3 Pro while significantly outperforming Claude Sonnet 4.5, Mistral Large 3, and Prime Intellect 3.
LEXam-IDK changes the game: it rewards correct answers (+1), penalizes wrong ones (-1), and gives 0 points for abstentions ("I don't know"). This scoring reveals which models know their limits.
Key findings:
- GPT-5.2 shows remarkable calibration with only a ~10-point trad→idk drop (88.85% → 78.19%), demonstrating strong baseline accuracy with minimal abstention
- Gemini 3 Pro sits statistically close (87.56% → 75.12%, within overlapping confidence intervals) but never abstains, resulting in a 12.44-point penalty
- A clear performance gap emerges with mid-tier models: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (16.64-point drop, 4.5% IDK rate) and Mistral Large (19.22-point drop, 2.3% IDK rate)
- Prime Intellect 3 liberally abstains (12.8% IDK rate) but starts from a weaker baseline (58.97%), collapsing to 30.69%
The data is clear: strong baseline accuracy with minimal abstention outperforms aggressive abstention strategies. For legal AI, knowing when to say "I don't know" matters—but knowing the right answer matters more.
Are higher IDK rates a bug or a feature in legal AI systems?

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool new meta-evaluation PostTrainBench: evaluating LLMs as they train LLMs.
PostTrainBench measures the ability of CLI agents to post-train pre-trained large language models (LLMs). In PostTrainBench, the agent's task is to improve the performance of a base LLM on a given benchmark. The agent is given access to an evaluation script and 10 hours on an H100 GPU. Performance is measured by the benchmark score of the post-trained LLM. This setup naturally evaluates an agent's ability to conduct AI R&D.
The researchers from ELLIS Institute Tübingen and Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems show that current CLI agents using leading frontier models can significantly improve small open LLMs over base performance, but still fall far short of a strong human post-training pipeline under similar tasks. Human-led post-training achieves an average score of 61.8 across four models (Qwen 3 1.7B, Qwen 3 4B, SmolLM3-3B, Gemma 3 4B IT) and five benchmarks (AIME 2025, BFCL, GPQA Main, GSM8K, and HumanEval), whereas the best agent (gpt-5.1-codex-max) reaches 34.9 and several other top agents remain close to the base-model average of 9, often not even using the full available 10-hour H100 budget.
Super cool work by @full__rank, @hrdkbhatnagar, @MatthiasBethge and @maksym_andr!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Great new post by @lvwerra summarizing the last seven years of progress since GPT-1!
He outlines how LLMs excel at coding because of extraordinarily rich public data (28M repositories, 1B+ commits annually), with targeted improvements rapidly making them useful for developers. Math became the next frontier, with models reaching olympiad-level performance primarily through curating huge high-quality datasets, rather than just scaling. Science presents a harder challenge: unlike math's text-based substrate, the actual scientific process (experiment design, failures, measurements) is rarely captured in accessible data, and synthetic data can't easily fill this gap since validation requires physical experiments.
I'd argue that law represents the next frontier beyond science, which may explain why frontier labs don't yet evaluate on legal benchmarks. While science faces data challenges, it retains a crucial advantage: experimental verifiability. Even with slow experiments in the absence of sophisticated simulators, we can still test hypotheses against physical reality. Law may prove even more intractable for LLMs. Validating legal reasoning often requires the expensive, time-consuming process of actual litigation, with no simulators available and outcomes depending on human judgment in ways that resist systematic verification.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool new benchmark from @MiniMax_AI: OctoCodingBench
Current coding agent benchmarks only measure whether tasks are completed, not whether agents follow the specified rules and constraints during the process. Users are frustrated when agents produce working code but violate explicit instructions like naming conventions, safety protocols, or team standards.
MiniMax introduces OctoCodingBench, which evaluates agents on both Check-level Success Rate (individual rule compliance) and Instance-level Success Rate (adherence to all rules simultaneously). This process-oriented approach measures whether agents follow constraints from system prompts, user queries, repository specifications, and project documentation.
Main findings:
- Models follow individual rules well but struggle combining them
- Instruction-following degrades significantly over multiple conversation turns
- Open-source models now rival top closed-source performance levels

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
End of last year @HuggingFace released FinePDFs, an enormous pretraining dataset of 475M PDFs on the web.
They also released a very illustrative blog post explaining much of the background related to PDF processing!
Below are my main takeaways.
- PDFs are especially important for long-context training (one in four PDFs is more than 1MB, the average is ~5.3k chars with the 95th percentile at ~68k)
- Less than 1% of documents in CommonCrawl are PDFs
- So much of the old internet is dead: about 2/3 before 2020
- Extraction speed is extremely important at this scale, so they trained a classifier to discriminate the PDFs that need OCR on a GPU leaving most of the PDFs for cheap CPU extraction
- LMDeploy is a promising inference framework alternative to vLLM if your model is supported
- They applied model-based filtering by labeling 300k samples with Qwen3‑235B‑A22B‑Instruct‑2507 and then distilling the labels to a small bert model (ModernBERT-large)
- The source distribution is extremely long-tail: There is many CDNs, government and legal sources (NRC, govinfo, state legislatures, Justia) and a solid block of science (arXiv, APS, Copernicus, MDPI)
Overall, creating a large-scale high-quality PDF dataset requires an intricate and long pipeline of many steps including many classifiers, extractors and cleaners.
The blog post is well worth a read!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
How to win best paper awards?
Find the idea
- have good research taste: know what to work on
- get good collaborators: catch mistakes early (how to get them? spend time into writing cold emails)
- read papers: why? 1. know what is possible, 2. what to do to get some result, 3. build on the paper
- ignore papers: don't be biased by bad ideas, hard to know what to discard and what to keep
- work on the most important problem in your field
- be fast: the exact same paper written 6 months earlier is the difference between groundbreaking and boring
- find your comparative advantage: e.g., I am good at data work but bad a modeling work
- get lucky: 1. you stumbled upon a good idea, 2. be uniquely positioned to solve the problem
Do the research
- get lucky again: the idea actually works
- kill papers that are not working: start on the hardest subproblem to derisk (I find this the hardest!)
- kill low impact papers: finish fast as blog posts or workshop papers
- reprioritize ruthlessly: immediately drop what you're working on and pivot to higher impact project (this is super hard because you have to be confident in your taste)
- put in unreasonable amounts of effort: good papers don't have poorly performed experiments
- have focus: on the core idea, nothing else
- the paper should be in a local optimum: no obvious improvements visible
Write it down
- have focus: on the core idea, nothing else
- know your reader: pick a particular one and write tailored to that reader
- your title is not so important: convince with the science, not clickbait
- your abstract is: convey sense of importance
- write a good intro: your results don't matter if the reader doesn't get the problem
- each figure must stand on its own: because most reader skim through the paper
- write a good conclusion: moment of reflection, not just abstract in past tense
- write well: read it out loud to catch things you would not otherwise
After writing
- get lucky one last time: 1. it's not too early, 2. it's still a hot topic, 3. nobody else did it first, 4. the committee likes it
- be persistent: often multiple submissions are required
Obviously don't just have the award as a goal, just use this to write impactful papers!
Great post by Nicholas Carlini!

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Nice blog post by Jack Morris on embedding models!
Main learnings:
- Embedding models have not been scaled up as much as generative models
- Scaling data does not work well naively because inevitably we will get (wrong) gradients on false negatives
- Human labels are super expensive, but we can approximate them with LLMs.
Full procedure:
1. Gather all the text pairs you can find.
2. For each query Q, filter the top-k using BM25 and embeddings. Gain some set of K documents {D_1, ..., D_K}, relevant to Q.
3. Run each pair (D_*, Q) through an LLM to figure out if D is truly a negative example or not.
4. Output: a perfectly-labeled retrieval dataset that's arbitrarily scalable.
5. Train the model using exact softmax and coordinate ascent.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
📰🎓 New extension to the Synthetic Data Playbook!
We trained 60 models to answer one question: does generator size actually matter for synthetic pretraining data? The answer is yes, but only if your student is big enough to notice.
We swept Gemma-3 generators (270M to 27B) across four student sizes (0.5B to 6.2B) and found:
- A 0.5B student squashes all generators into a tiny band (spread: 0.004). It literally can't tell good data from great data.
- At 2.9B, three tiers emerge: 270M is clearly worst, 1B sits in the middle, 4B+ generators form a top group.
- Going past 2.9B to 6.2B doesn't widen the gap much further. 2.9B is the sweet spot.
The big takeaway: if you're evaluating synthetic data with a small proxy model, your conclusions might be wrong. We thought generator size didn't matter past 1B. Turns out our 1.7B student was just too small to see the difference. A 2.9B student reveals quality gaps that the 1.7B student compressed into noise.
Pick your evaluation model carefully. It changes what you can measure.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Happy to share that our paper "Parity-Aware Byte-Pair Encoding: Improving Cross-lingual Fairness in Tokenization" was accepted to #ACL2026 in San Diego 🇺🇸!
When you use ChatGPT or Claude, you pay per token. But did you know that tokenization is wildly unfair across languages? Standard algorithms like BPE learn by counting what appears most frequently in training data, which overwhelmingly favors English and other high-resource languages. The result: speakers of lower-resource languages see their text split into more tokens, paying higher API costs for the same message.
Vocabulary utilization measures what fraction of a tokenizer's vocabulary actually gets used for each language. When utilization is low, the model has failed to allocate meaningful tokens to that language, fragmenting words into inefficient subwords.
We introduce Parity-Aware BPE, which at every step asks: "Which language is currently getting the worst compression?" It then selects merges that specifically help that language. The result is dramatically fairer vocabulary allocation across high, medium, and low-resource languages compared to Classical BPE.
Best part? Models trained with our tokenizer perform just as well on downstream tasks, while achieving near-perfect parity in tokenization costs. Same performance, fairer access.
Joint work with @negarforoutan, @clara__meister, @DebjitPaul2, @sina_ahm, @ABosselut, and @RicoSennrich.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Synthetic Data Playbook update!
TLDR: Most diversity scores don't predict synthetic-data quality. G-Vendi is the exception.
I added four diversity metrics across 83 synthetic-pretraining experiments: Vendi Score, mean intra-set cosine similarity, and near-duplicate rate (all on bge-base-en-v1.5 sentence embeddings), plus G-Vendi from the Prismatic Synthesis paper. The selling point if any of them works: rank a candidate rephrasing recipe from 1000 generated samples, instead of generating millions of tokens and training a student model end-to-end.
The three semantic metrics fall apart on aggregate downstream performance. Vendi correlates negatively (ρ = −0.21), mean cosine similarity positively (ρ = +0.23, but that's just −Vendi by construction), near-duplicate rate essentially zero. None of them is a usable overall predictor.
G-Vendi flips the script. Instead of asking "do these samples look different?", it asks "would training on each of them push the model's weights in different directions?". You backprop the cross-entropy loss through a frozen proxy LLM (I used Qwen3-0.6B), sketch the resulting gradient, L2-normalise and then take the Vendi Score in that feature space. Across the same 83 experiments, G-Vendi correlates positively with the macro score (ρ = +0.26) and is the single best predictor for reasoning of any metric I tested (ρ = +0.38), beating every quality classifier and semantic-diversity variant.
But none of this displaces DCLM-difference. Even G-Vendi explains only ~7% of variance on the macro score, while DCLM-difference (output minus input quality score) still wins overall (ρ = +0.61). Diversity metrics complement quality classifiers, they don't replace them. The shortcut around training-and-evaluating still doesn't exist.

New FinePhrase result: the best synthetic-to-real ratio for pretraining isn't 50/50.
Quick context: FinePhrase is our open 486B-token synthetic pretraining dataset. We take FineWeb-Edu web text, rephrase it with a small 1.7B model (SmolLM2) into four structured formats (FAQs, math problems, tables, tutorials), and then train on a mix of original and synthetic data. The whole recipe came out of 90 controlled pretraining experiments.
The new question we tackled: how much of that mix should actually be synthetic? We swept the synthetic fraction from 10% to 90% for each format. Every format's optimum sits higher than the uniform 50/50, and it's format-dependent: tables peak at 70% synthetic, math at 80%, FAQ and tutorials at 60%. The curves climb to their peak and then plateau rather than collapsing, so there's a wide safe band and no sign of the "too much synthetic = model collapse" failure mode.
This also sets a new state of the art among synthetic pretraining data. Our best config (tables at 70% synthetic) is 31% better and reaches the same quality 3.2x faster than REWIRE, the strongest rephrasing baseline, which used a 70B-parameter model. We get there with a 1.7B rephraser that also generates tokens roughly 30x cheaper.
A caveat: these results are at small scale (1.7B parameters, 21B training tokens) so might not transfer to larger training runs.

summary:
New update to the Synthetic Data Playbook: how much of our results is just luck?
Quick refresher: the Synthetic Data Playbook is our open guide to turning noisy web text into state-of-the-art pretraining data, by finding the right prompts, rephrasing models, and infrastructure.
The whole playbook rests on comparing training runs. Recipe A scores a bit higher than recipe B, so A wins. But every score comes from a single run, and training is random (the weight initialization and the order the data arrives both involve a dice roll). So a fair question to ask before trusting any of it: how much does the score move if we change nothing but the random seeds?
We added a dedicated check to find out. We took our headline recipe (FineWeb-Edu-HQ blended 50/50 with table-formatted synthetic data) and the raw baseline it beats, and retrained each one nine times, sweeping the init seed and the data-order seed in a 3×3 grid. Then we repeated the whole thing at four model sizes from 0.5B to 6.2B. 72 from-scratch runs, just to measure noise.
What we found:
- The noise floor is tiny. Scores reproduce to about ±0.002 (roughly 1% wobble) at every model size. The bar doesn't grow as models get bigger.
- The synthetic-data win is not luck. The gain over the raw baseline is 14 to 26 times larger than that noise. There is simply no seed you could pick that erases it.
- Which dice matter? The model's initialization matters more than the order it sees the data. Data ordering is consistently the smallest source of variance.
Synthetic data even stabilizes training. The mixed recipe was more reproducible than the raw-web baseline at every scale.
- This lines up with what the broader community has found training models from scratch across seeds (MultiBERTs, PolyPythias, DataDecide), and it's exactly why we evaluate in cloze format, which is known to cut this kind of measurement noise for small models.
Two things this number doesn't cover. That ±0.002 bar is an aggregate number. Individual benchmarks are far noisier (a 1-point move on DROP is just noise, while the same move on HellaSwag is real), and we only ran the full seed grid on one synthetic recipe, so we treat it as a rule of thumb rather than a guarantee.
The takeaway: the gaps we report in the playbook are real signal, not seed roulette. New interactive chart in the post lets you flip between the scores, the per-seed training curves, and a breakdown of where the variance comes from.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
DeepSeek V4 Pro goes from 0 to 5% all-pass rate on the new Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark, doubling GPT 5.5 performance!
Harness-optimization makes open models useful for super hard real-world legal work!
Read the blog post:
Quoting @akshay_pachaar
Don't train the model, evolve the harness.
I read a brilliant blog post from Hugging Face where they took a frozen open model scoring 0% on a hard legal agent benchmark, left its weights alone, and let an automated loop rewrite only the code around it.
That code layer is the harness, the runtime wrapper that feeds the model context, runs its tool calls, and decides when a run ends.
By the time the loop finished, the system had essentially matched Sonnet 4.6 on the benchmark's headline metric, at roughly 7x lower cost per task. Zero weights changed.
The gain existed because of where the model was failing. The judge only grades files saved in the right place under the exact requested filename, and the model kept doing the legal analysis correctly, then saving it under the wrong name, dropping it in a scratch folder, or never writing it at all.
So the 0% was never measuring legal reasoning. It was measuring the harness.
Hand-tuning that layer is slow and model-specific, so they automated it. A Claude proposer adds exactly one mechanism per iteration, and an outer loop keeps it only if it clearly beats the current best, so accepted mechanisms compound.
What the loop discovered says a lot about where agents actually fail.
→ The biggest single gain was file handling, not intelligence. An automatic step that lands the deliverable exactly where the judge expects it beat every prompt change, with zero extra model tokens.
→ Code fixes transferred across models, prompt playbooks did not. The same harness lifted a smaller model from the same family by 14 points, but the tuned prompts hurt a different model family on tasks it could already finish.
→ The harness mattered more than anything else. Same model, same judge, same tasks, and five different harnesses scored anywhere between 3.5% and 80.1%.
The gains do eventually flatten, and the remaining misses look like real capability gaps. At some point the wrapper runs out of tricks and the model has to carry the work.
But the lesson holds. A benchmark score measures the model and its harness together, and until the harness is fixed, it's impossible to know which one failed.

I also wrote a deep dive on agent harness engineering a while back, covering the orchestration loop, tools, memory, context management, and everything that turns a stateless LLM into a capable agent.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] We just got an award at #ACL2026 for our Parity-Aware BPE paper!
When AI systems process text, they first break it into chunks called tokens. The standard method for deciding how to chunk text (called BPE) learns from frequency: chunks that appear often in the training data get treated efficiently.
Since training data is dominated by languages like English, those languages get compact, sensible tokenizations, while lower-resource languages end up chopped into many more tokens, often in ways that ignore how the language actually works.
This matters practically: more tokens means more computation and higher costs, so speakers of underrepresented languages literally pay more to use the same AI systems.
We propose a fix called Parity-aware BPE. Instead of always picking the chunk that helps compression overall (which mostly benefits dominant languages), our version repeatedly asks: which language is currently getting the worst deal?
Then it picks the chunk that most helps *that* language. It sacrifices a tiny bit of overall efficiency in exchange for fairness across languages.
The results: inequality between languages (measured with the Gini coefficient, the same statistic used for income inequality) drops by up to 89%, while overall compression barely suffers and the AI models trained with it perform just as well.
Great to have been part of an amazing author team: @negarforoutan, @clara__meister, @DebjitPaul2, @sina_ahm, @ABosselut,

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Super influential and well written at the same time as usual!
Quoting @a1zhang
Transformers struggle to generalize to tasks they were not explicitly trained on. Instead, we propose in 2026 that it is the job of the harness to generalize through composition.
We observe a powerful property when training RLMs: for tasks with shared structure that look different, the root model naturally learns the same trajectory, meaning it views the two task trajectories as the same! In other words, the Transformer does not need additional generalization capabilities to transfer capabilities from one task to the other, the harness induces it.
We find that well-designed harnesses form a quotient set over task trajectories, meaning their individual LLM calls can see structurally “similar” tasks as near-identical, token-for-token! Harnesses can effectively generalize for the Transformer during training, without relying on any intrinsic generalization capability from the model.
For example, RLMs can see problems of different lengths as the same: we show that RLMs can train exclusively on short tasks, and fully generalize to similar but unseen tasks 8-32x longer because it produces near identical trajectories for both.
Taking this further, we show that tasks across different domains (e.g. math solutions vs. essay writing) that share a decomposition strategy exhibit the same generalization effect. RLMs can train on the problem of finding which essays belong to the same author and improve performance on finding math problems that share similar solutions.

summary:
[1/3] Codex is overoptimised for large models: it ranks 2nd out of 10 for GLM 5.2 but drops to 9th place for Gemma-4!
Almost all the effort in this field goes into tuning the weights. We wanted to know how much of the final number is decided by the harness wrapped around them instead, so we ran 10 coding agent harnesses against two models on SWE-bench Pro.
A lot, it turns out. Swapping the harness moves pass@1 from 23% to 52% on GLM-5.2, and from 15% to 36% on Gemma 4 26B-A4B: a wider gap than most model releases buy you.
And the ranking does not transfer. The rank correlation between the two models' harness leaderboards is -0.05, which is to say: none.
Codex is not alone in this. Every harness shipped by a model vendor drops on the small model — Codex 2nd to 9th, Claude Code 3rd to 7th, Qwen Code 4th to 6th — while the model-agnostic ones climb: crush 7th to 1st, opencode 8th to 2nd, pi 9th to 4th.
The clearest case is crush, 7th on GLM-5.2 and 1st on Gemma 4. Run the identical scaffold on both and the small model wins by 4 points at a twelfth of the price, $0.30 per task against $3.61.
Gemma 4's best harness beats GLM-5.2's four worst. A 26B model in the right scaffold is not far off a 744B model in the wrong one.
Cost per solved task: $0.84 for Gemma 4 + crush at 36%. The cheapest GLM-5.2 setup that scores as well is openclaw at 38%, for $7.05.
Output tokens per task span 16k to 621k across harnesses: a 39x spread in what you pay for, buying a 2x spread in what you get.
97% of input tokens are re-sent conversation prefix, so prompt caching is super important.
The setup: every harness run against both models on the same 250 SWE-bench Pro tasks, one rollout each, priced at list API rates for the tokens each one actually spent. In the plot, a dark ring means the pairing sits on the Pareto frontier across both models and a faded dot means you could score higher for less elsewhere; 2 of the 10 harnesses (goose and hermes) are left out of the figure for legibility

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
I really think we need a centralized organisation that acts as a source of truth for benchmarking!
And with the recent surge in importance of harnesses this gets even more important imo.
Let me explain why.
Already back when we just evaluated LLMs we had a reproducibility crisis.
System prompt, quantization, temperature, top_p, reasoning effort (not even standardized across providers), and other variables can all drastically change performance.
There are so many sources of variance that most runs are not comparable even when targeting the same benchmark!
So we need really standardization to compare models confidently.
Adding harnesses into the mix makes this even more unwieldy. Suddenly we add a whole new source of variance, not even speaking of the infrastructure where we run tasks, differently defined tools, etc.
I only see two options:
1) We need to converge on very clear evaluation standards as a field including an open evaluation harness and reproducible reasoning effort, or
2) we need one central organisation emerging that provides the necessary infrastructure to compare models across benchmarks and harnesses
Quoting @joelniklaus
We need @ArtificialAnlys for harnesses!
Cool to see this kind of interest in harness evaluation, makes it clear to me that this is still an underexplored area.
We have lots of evaluations that compare LLMs but this gets less and less meaningful just by itself because the harness it operates in makes such a huge difference. We need to know what harness LLMs are evaluated in and standardize it if we want to really get the full picture of how good an LLM performs for a task.
Ideally, we go a step further and select a few top harnesses and evaluate each model inside all of them and measure the spread similar to the recent Qwen 3.8 release.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
For Muse-Glimmer-30B, harness choice is a no-brainer: OpenCode sits at the high-performance, low-cost edge.
To test this, I evaluated 10 agent harnesses on the same 50 held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks for three trials each, producing 1,500 scored attempts.
TB2.1 tests whether an agent can complete software tasks inside an isolated terminal environment, with each task’s verifier deciding success.
At the two edges, OpenCode reached 41.3% pass@1 at $0.71 list cost per attempt, while OpenClaw reached 20.7% at $1.82.
That gap compounds into the most useful result: $1.73 per solved task for OpenCode versus $8.80 for OpenClaw, a 5.1× difference with identical model weights.
Qwen Code provides another revealing comparison, nearly matching OpenCode at 40.0% while costing 1.95× more per attempt at $1.39.
The token data explains much of this cost spread: depending on the harness, average usage ranged from 1.78M to 5.12M input tokens per attempt while output averaged only 17k–36k.
Against the model’s 131k context window, that input equals roughly 14–39 complete windows sent during one attempt.
Output contributed only 3–4% of list-price cost, making repeated context the main economic variable.
Caching changes the absolute bill substantially: for the six harnesses with complete cache data, 96–98% of input was served from cache, reducing estimated cost by 5.5–6.4×.
The plot shows OpenCode’s $0.71 list-price estimate, while applying the measured cache discount lowers it to $0.13 per attempt, an 82% reduction.
Even after that adjustment, the central result holds, with pi and OpenCode still defining the Pareto frontier.
Together, these results suggest that context handling and cache use matter more economically than how much text the agent produces.
The benchmark contains 50 unique tasks with three repeated trials per task, so small pass-rate gaps should not be treated as definitive rankings.
Under the hood, the architecture separated benchmark execution from model serving: each Harbor attempt ran as an isolated Slurm CPU job, while Muse-Glimmer-30B inference stayed remote on Hugging Face Inference Providers through Together.
Harbor handled each harness’s lifecycle and collected its verifier result, while a shared wiring layer connected compatible harnesses directly and translated Anthropic Messages or OpenAI Responses into Chat Completions where required.
This separation also makes the setup reusable, because switching benchmarks mainly requires a new frozen split and task-image import while leaving the harness wiring unchanged.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
More cool work on automated research replication!
They introduce Replica, a 310-task benchmark where agents must recreate redacted results figures from 100 ML and AI-for-science papers under a 60-minute, limited-GPU budget; a task-specific LLM rubric judges both the plot and the scientific quality of the underlying experiment.
The authors post-train a 27B model, Faraday, with GRPO to orchestrate a coding agent, reporting higher average replication scores than Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5/Codex: 0.856 vs. 0.828/0.796 on ML tasks and 0.791 vs. 0.748/0.729 on held-out AI-for-science tasks.
The core claim is that training on underspecified replication work teaches an agent more rigorous, transferable scientific behavior such as implementing the actual mechanism rather than faking expected outputs.
I found it quite interesting that a small model (Faraday) can direct a much larger one (GPT 5.5).
They also found that recent papers are harder to replicate possibly due to recent papers needing more compute.

summary:
Speculative Programmatic Tool Calling is such a neat and clean idea!
Most agent harnesses wait for the model to finish generating a REPL program before executing its tool calls. sPTC parses the program while it streams, pre-launches safe calls in a shadow REPL, and reuses the result if the final program makes that call. It can also parallelize independent calls that the generated code wrote as blocking. In effect, it is a small JIT layer for agent programs.
The first RLM experiments show up to roughly 1.2x speedups, depending heavily on the trajectory and tool latency.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
AI Research Preference Models from FAIR sparked a lively discussion in the Hugging Face journal club yesterday!
The paper starts from the idea that AI agents have made proposing and implementing research ideas much cheaper: an agent can generate many plausible code changes or experiment plans quickly, but training and evaluating each one can still cost hours or days of scarce GPU time. That makes research taste—deciding which ideas are genuinely promising, which are redundant, and which are not worth pursuing—an increasingly important bottleneck; the authors call this research preference.
Their solution is a Research Preference Model (RPM), which sits between idea generation and expensive execution: the agent proposes several candidate experiments, then the RPM selects the one most likely to lead somewhere useful. An inference-only RPM inspects plans, code, and prior experiment results; an agentic RPM additionally runs small, cheap pilot experiments to gather evidence before choosing.
The broader intuition is similar to why frontier AI labs value exceptional researchers so highly: implementation capacity alone is not enough when there are countless things one could build; unusually good judgment about what to try, what evidence to trust, and where the hidden leverage is can determine how efficiently compute and teams translate into progress. The paper operationalizes a narrow, testable version of that judgment—ranking candidate ML experiments—and finds that it raises AIRS-Bench performance from 0.684 to 0.711 with reasoning alone and to 0.729 with pilot experiments, while reaching the baseline’s final result in roughly 15 rather than 24 hours.
It also has fun parallels to Monte Carlo Tree Search, my favorite algorithm :)

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Cool work by Sebastian Nagl, @matgrabmair and team!
BenGER is a benchmark for testing whether AI systems can solve German-law problems using the structured legal reasoning method taught in law school: identify the relevant rule, define its elements, apply the facts, and reach a conclusion. It includes 596 long, exam-style case tasks—581 from a public legal-education journal and 15 newly written Benchathon tasks—plus 531 shorter questions about legal principles. The Benchathon portion also contains 220 human-written answers, both unaided and written with optional AI assistance, allowing direct human–AI comparison.
Across 12 systems, closed flagship models like Gemini-3.1-Pro, Opus-4.7, and GPT-5.4 performed best, while the strongest open-weight model, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, was competitive with smaller closed systems but behind the flagships.
The clearest practical result is that people using AI scored 15.7 points higher out of 100 than people working without it, placing human–AI work roughly in the closed-flagship range. Their LLM-based grader correlated reasonably well with blind human graders (r=0.76), though the authors stress that the human-review sample is small and the judge should support human assessment and not replace it.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Same weights. $50 of harness search. 3x on Terminal-Bench.
We optimized the OpenCode harness for GPT-OSS-20B (high reasoning) with a
meta-harness: an agent that reads failures, patches the harness, and validates the improvement. The model never changed.
On held-out Terminal-Bench 2.1, the optimized harness scored 14.8%, up from
OpenCode's 4.8%. That is 3.08x, from $49.97 of API credits.
Three harness fixes carried most of the gain:
- i7, verify before stopping: the model often edited code and ended the session
without testing it. The harness gives it another turn to run the code.
- i14, continue announced actions: the model would say "now run X" and then stop. The harness keeps the session going so it runs X.
- i23, repair malformed tool calls: one extra `]` made OpenCode reject otherwise
valid commands. The harness repairs that clear-cut error.
How the meta-harness ran:
1. Start: stock OpenCode v1.18.13 + GPT-OSS-20B scored 8.5% on the dev split.
2. Iterate: Claude Code (Opus 5 max) reads the failed dev trajectories and proposes one patch. We build it and run it once per dev task, paired against the current parent.
3. Validate: candidates that clear a pre-registered margin get a 5-trial validation.
They become the new parent only if their validated score surpasses the current one.
4. Stop: the loop ended after 23 iterations and about 2.4k dev attempts, when the $50 search budget was spent.
Takeaway: pre-training puts capability in the weights, and post-training makes that capability usable. Harness optimization continues the same work at inference time, turning the model's behavior into more completed tasks. Same weights, 3x the finished tasks.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
Releasing LEXam-hard, a subset of the hardest open questions from LEXam.
LEXam is a bilingual legal reasoning benchmark built from 340 University of Zurich law exams covering Swiss, European and international law.
We scored all 2,541 open questions with the 16 open models from SwissLegalEvals, then defined difficulty as each question's mean score among the top seven models and kept the 546 below 50. DeepSeek V4 Flash screened that pool for questions that depended on missing material, dropping 52. Fable 5.1 reviewed those 52 and restored 24 that named the facts or public document they needed, leaving 518 questions.
Some low-scoring questions require a specific court decision, statute or scholarly position that the model does not know; we kept these because a legal research tool can help. We removed questions that referred to missing material, such as "see exercise 4.1" or "the above advertisement."
On LEXam-hard, Inkling leads at 40.8, down from 67.7 on the full set. Every one of the 16 models loses 9 to 30 points, and the spread between the best and worst model shrinks from 43 points to 25.
LEXam-hard concentrates the fifth of the exam where current open models have the most room to improve and legal research tools can matter.

clean_summary:
Pre-pretraining (PPT) means training a language model briefly on synthetic, non-natural language data before the usual pretraining on natural language. Earlier studies looked at small models and limited token budgets, so it was unclear if PPT helps at larger scales.

Joël Niklaus and colleagues scale PPT up to 7 billion parameters and 100 billion tokens across multiple data mixtures and tasks. They find that PPT remains beneficial at this scale, saving at least 21 billion pretraining tokens for a 3 billion parameter model. This suggests PPT can improve training efficiency even for very large models.

summary:
Super excited to share that FinePhrase has been selected as an Oral Spotlight at #COLM2026!
I will present on Wednesday afternoon next week. First in Oral Session 4 at 3:30PM PT and then in Poster Session 4 between 4:30 and 6:30PM (Poster F-4-126).
If you're in SF, I am looking forward to seeing you at the talk or in the poster session!
What is FinePhrase all about?
Synthetic data is a standard component in training large language models, yet systematic comparisons across design dimensions, including rephrasing strategy, generator model, and source data, remain absent.
We conduct extensive controlled experiments, generating over one trillion tokens, to identify critical factors in rephrasing web text into synthetic pretraining data.
Our results reveal that structured output formats, such as tables, math problems, FAQs, and tutorials, consistently outperform both curated web baselines and prior synthetic methods.
Notably, increasing the size of the generator model beyond 1B parameters provides no additional benefit.
Our analysis also demonstrates that the selection of the original data used for mixing substantially influences performance.
By applying our findings, we develop FinePhrase, a 486-billion-token open dataset of rephrased web text.
We show that FinePhrase outperforms all existing synthetic data baselines while reducing generation costs by up to 30 times.
We provide the dataset, all prompts, and the generation framework to the research community.

title: Joël Niklaus @ CoLM (@joelniklaus)
summary:
If you've used the same model in different harnesses, you've probably noticed it behaves very differently in each.
Our new technical deep dive shows how to fix this by training the model with RL inside the harnesses themselves:
In some cases, the gap is huge: before any training, LFM2.5-2.6B solved 62% of tasks in Mini-SWE-Agent but only 33% in Claude Code 😢
The obvious fix is to train inside the harness, but this isn't simple because the harness controls the agent loop, so the trainer never sees the exact tokens the model produced. We solved this with:
> a capture proxy in OpenEnv that records tokens + logprobs from harnesses
> @harborframework for the tasks and sandboxes
> TRL's super fast async GRPO trainer
Training LFM2.5-2.6B across four harnesses took it from 42% → 54% on held-out tasks, with gains in every harness and 31% fewer tool calls on tasks it already solved 🔥
Training in OpenCode alone mostly improved ... OpenCode 😅
Huge kudos to @adithya_s_k for leading this, and to @QGallouedec @DirhousssiAmine @SergioPaniego @ben_burtenshaw for enabling multi-harness training in TRL & OpenEnv!

clean_summary:
Joël Niklaus highlights a keynote about Meta-Harness and WHALE, two frameworks that improve how large language models interact with their environment. Meta-Harness offers an end-to-end way to optimize model harnesses, which are the external code controlling model behavior.

WHALE takes this further by alternating between updating the model's weights and improving the harness code itself. This joint optimization leads to better AI agent performance, as shown in their experiments.
